title: The third and fourth weeks
hook: walking with Christ through the passion, then the joy of resurrection

segments.voice: Yesterday, two standards: two banners, two ladders. Your line was under his banner. Did you hand someone the credit you could have kept? Day one thousand one hundred forty-five.

"Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." Paul wrote that to the Christians in Rome, about how to treat one another. The last two weeks of Ignatius of Loyola's Spiritual Exercises ask for something close to it, with one friend at the center. In the third week, the one praying walks with Jesus through his passion: the supper, the garden, the trial, the cross, the tomb. In the fourth week, through the resurrection and the days after. Two very different weeks, and one request running through both: to be with him in whatever he's going through. Today: the third and fourth weeks.

In the third week, Ignatius asks for a grace that can surprise people. Not to explain the cross. Not even, first of all, to feel guilty. He asks for sorrow with Christ in sorrow: grief, tears, an inner pain at the pain Christ bears for the one praying. It's the prayer of someone sitting beside a friend in a hospital room. He even suggests noticing how, in the passion, the divinity seems to hide itself, and lets the human Jesus suffer terribly. So the one praying stays near and keeps watch, the way Jesus asked his friends to watch with him in the garden. In the fourth week, the grace turns over. Now it's to be glad, and to rejoice, because of the glory and joy of Christ risen. John's Gospel gives that moment one plain sentence. In the King James: "Then were the disciples glad, when they saw the Lord." Ignatius also asks the one praying to watch how the risen Christ goes about consoling his friends, the way one friend comforts another. Here's what makes these weeks hard. Sorrow on someone else's behalf, and joy on someone else's behalf, both mean stepping out of your own center. The joy of the fourth week isn't about your own good news. It's gladness that things have gone well for him. That's an ordinary human skill too, and a tricky one. Crying at a sad film can come easier than being glad, really glad, when a friend gets the thing you wanted. The church calendar keeps both in one shape: Good Friday, and then Easter.

Here's the practice: make room for both sorrow and joy, on someone else's behalf. Settle. First, stand for a while near the cross, or near someone you know who is suffering right now. Don't try to fix anything. Just stay. Then, partway through, turn. Go to the garden on the first morning, or bring to mind someone whose life just went well. Let any gladness be for them, not for you. If you pray, you can hold both before God. If not, notice how each one sits in your body. The bell holds the time.
The third and fourth weeks. The passion, then the resurrection, prayed as a friend: sorrow with Christ in sorrow, and joy with Christ in joy.
